She then leaves the kitchen to take a phone call that lasts about fifteen minutes. The mug sits on the counter the entire time, undisturbed, in a normally warm room. When she returns she peers into the mug before drinking.

must_identify: ice melts when surrounded by hot liquid
fifteen minutes is far longer than needed for one cube in hot tea
no replenishment of ice
the cube has fully melted into the tea

title: Domino at edge of table
question: Where does the last domino end up? Answer in one short phrase.
input: Elena lines up twenty dominoes in a straight row across her dining table, each standing on its narrow end and spaced so that toppling one will knock the next. The final domino in the row stands with half its base hanging over the table's edge; the other half rests on the wood. Elena flicks the first domino. The chain reaction proceeds smoothly all the way down the line until the last domino is struck.

must_identify: struck domino tips forward off the table
unsupported objects fall to the floor
the table edge offers no barrier
final resting place is the floor below

title: Bicycle leaned on wet grass
question: What happens to the bicycle? Answer in one short phrase.
input: Tomás rides his bicycle to a park picnic and props it up by leaning the left pedal against a slim metal pole stuck loosely in soft, rain-soaked grass. The bicycle has no kickstand. The pole is the only thing keeping the bike from tipping. Tomás joins his friends at a blanket fifteen meters away. A breeze gradually loosens the pole, which slowly leans away from the bike until it slides free from the pedal entirely.

the pole was the only support
removal of support means no balance
the bike topples sideways onto the grass

title: Paper boat in stream

input: Anya folds a small paper boat and sets it gently on the surface of a clear, steadily flowing creek that runs from the hills above her village down toward the river in the valley. current flows from hills to valley
no wind or obstacles to override the flow
boat travels downstream

title: Heavy box on thin shelf

input: Renting a new apartment, Cal mounts a single decorative shelf of thin pine, rated by its label for two kilograms maximum, on two small drywall anchors. load greatly exceeds capacity

shelf will pull free or break

input: Metallurgist's notebook: 'If an alloy contains chromium above 10%, it forms a passive oxide layer that prevents pitting in saltwater immersion tests.' the tag does not match the register, so the conjoined consequent fails

structural review implies Class B permit
Hala's greenhouse is 34 ft, triggering the chain
the 28-ft exemption is a distractor

title: Frost and harvest delay
question: Will the Hadley orchard's apple harvest yield drop by at least 30%? Answer yes or no.
input: Agronomy notes from the regional extension office: If overnight temperatures fall below -2°C in early April, then the apple blossoms suffer cellular damage. blossom damage implies 30% yield drop
Hadley experienced -4°C, satisfying first antecedent

input: Trade regulation 14: If a software product uses key lengths greater than 256 bits, it is classified as munitions-grade. A separate consumer-protection rule requires open-source disclosure for products sold domestically. munitions-grade implies need for export license

open-source disclosure rule is a distractor

title: Volcanic ash and flights
question: Will authorities impose a no-fly zone over Mount Sereno's flight corridor?
input: Aviation safety briefing: When a stratovolcano erupts explosively, ash plumes reach the upper troposphere within hours. microfractures imply mandatory closure within 24 hours

input: Reviewer 2 thinks the submitted paper's main claim is wrong. He lists in his report the three experiments that support the authors' claim and the two that he believes contain a confound. He explicitly writes: 'If the authors can rule out the confound in experiments 4 and 5, my objection dissolves.' He cites two prior papers that contradict his own view and engages with them on the merits, ultimately disagreeing but acknowledging they raise the bar for his objection. He recommends major revision, not rejection.

must_identify: reviewer has a prior view
he engages with both supporting and disconfirming evidence
he states conditions under which he would change his mind
disagreement alone is not confirmation bias

title: Coach and the favored player
question: What is the primary reasoning flaw? Answer in two words.
input: Coach Reyna believes Devon is her best midfielder. She keeps a notebook tracking Devon's successful passes (47 last month) but does not log his turnovers. She tracks rival midfielder Sam's turnovers (12) but not his successful passes. When Devon loses possession in the final minute of a loss, Reyna tells reporters 'the back line failed him.' When Sam loses possession, she benches him for a half. The team's analytics show Sam has a higher pass-completion rate; Reyna has not opened the analytics dashboard this season.

must_identify: prior belief Devon is best
asymmetric tracking (successes for Devon, failures for Sam)
reinterpreting Devon's failures as others' fault
ignoring available disconfirming analytics

title: Astronomer at a fresh dataset
question: Does this passage demonstrate confirmation bias? Answer yes or no.
input: Dr. Okafor hypothesizes that a faint signal in her data is from a distant pulsar. She runs the standard pulsar pipeline and gets a marginal detection. She also runs three null tests designed to fail if the signal is instrumental: a time-shuffle, an off-source comparison, and a frequency-scrambled control. Two of the three null tests show the signal vanishes as expected for a real source; the third produces an anomalous residual. She reports all four results in her preprint and flags the anomalous residual as a reason for caution before claiming detection.

must_identify: prior hypothesis (pulsar)
deliberate disconfirming tests run
all results, including disconfirming, are reported
no asymmetric weighting

title: Conspiracy forum moderator
question: What reasoning flaw is shown? Answer in two words.
input: Forum moderator Kade is sure a tech company plants stories in the press. He pins every article that paints the company favorably as 'evidence of media capture.' When a major exposé criticizes the company harshly, he posts that this is 'controlled opposition designed to look balanced.' When a neutral feature appears, he calls it 'soft propaganda.' Every possible coverage outcome — positive, negative, neutral — is filed as supporting his theory. He has never specified what coverage pattern would count against his hypothesis. He has not examined coverage of any other company for comparison.

must_identify: prior belief of media capture
every outcome reinterpreted as supporting
no specified disconfirming criterion
no comparison case examined

title: Vintage watch auction estimate
question: Was the final price distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: An auctioneer opens bidding on a vintage watch by announcing, 'Let's start at $50,000—a number I picked because today is May 15.' Bidders react, and the watch ultimately sells for $42,000. The buyer remarks it was 'a steal compared to the opening.' Independent horologists who appraised similar models last month valued the watch at $18,000 to $22,000 based on movement, condition, and provenance.

must_identify: the $50,000 opening was arbitrary (chosen for the date)
the $42,000 final price was framed relative to the opening
independent appraisals placed value at $18,000-$22,000
the final figure was pulled toward the arbitrary anchor

title: Charity donation suggestion
question: Was Maria's donation amount influenced by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: A fundraising letter begins, 'Most donors give $500 or more.' Recipients then choose their gift. Maria, who typically donates $40 to local charities, sends $180 this time. Internal records reveal the '$500' figure was invented by a marketing intern with no supporting data. Maria later says she felt $180 was modest 'compared to what others give.'

must_identify: the $500 reference was fabricated/arbitrary
Maria's gift was framed relative to that figure
her usual baseline was $40
$180 represents an upward pull toward the anchor

title: Used car negotiation benchmark
question: Was Jordan's final price distorted by anchoring on the sticker? Answer yes or no.
input: Before visiting a used car lot, Jordan pulled three recent sales of the exact model and trim, averaging $14,200. The dealer's sticker read $19,800. Jordan offered $14,500 citing his comparable sales data, and after the dealer countered at $17,000, Jordan walked away. He returned days later when the dealer accepted $14,400.

must_identify: Jordan derived his offer from independent comparable sales
the sticker price did not pull his final figure
his final price ($14,400) matches his independent benchmark ($14,200)
the sticker is present but did not influence the judgment

title: Salary negotiation opener
question: Was the accepted salary distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: During a job interview, the recruiter mentions, 'The previous candidate asked for $185,000, though that role had different requirements.' The applicant, who had researched the position's market range at $110,000 to $125,000, ends up requesting $160,000 and accepting $150,000. He tells a friend the offer felt 'reasonable given where we started.'

must_identify: the $185,000 figure was introduced first and was acknowledged as not directly relevant
market research suggested $110,000-$125,000
the applicant's request and acceptance were framed relative to the opener
the final salary shifted upward toward the anchor

title: Wine list pricing pattern
question: Did the $400 listing anchor the patrons' choice? Answer yes or no.
input: A restaurant wine list places a $400 bottle at the top. Most patrons end up ordering the $90 bottle, calling it 'the sensible choice.' A wine consultant notes the $90 bottle wholesales for $14, while comparable restaurants in the neighborhood price equivalent bottles at $45 to $55. The owner privately admits the $400 listing was added 'to make everything else look affordable.'

must_identify: the $400 bottle was placed deliberately as a reference
comparable restaurants charge $45-$55 for similar bottles
patrons evaluated $90 relative to $400
the $90 judgment was pulled upward by the anchor

title: Property tax appeal estimate
question: Was the new assessment distorted by anchoring on the prior assessment? Answer yes or no.
input: An assessor reviews a home and notes the prior year's assessment of $312,000. She then runs a fresh comparative market analysis using six recent neighborhood sales, computes a value of $298,000, and submits that figure. The homeowner argues the new figure was 'just adjusted slightly down from last year.'

must_identify: the new figure came from independent comparative market analysis
six recent sales served as the basis
the prior assessment was not used as the reference
the homeowner's framing is mistaken

title: Population guess after spinner
question: Were the participants' estimates distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: A psychology demonstration spins a wheel that lands on 65 in front of participants. They are then asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. The group's median answer is 45%. A separate group, shown a wheel that landed on 10, gives a median answer of 25%. The wheel outcomes are random and unrelated to UN membership.

must_identify: the wheel numbers were random and unrelated to the question
the spin number preceded the estimate
groups shown different anchors gave systematically different answers
estimates were pulled toward the arbitrary anchor

title: Antique vase appraisal
question: Was the appraiser's figure distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: An owner tells an appraiser, 'My grandmother insured this vase for $25,000 in 1978.' The appraiser examines the piece, references current auction databases, applies condition adjustments, and concludes the vase is worth $3,200 today. She explains the 1978 insurance figure reflects a different era's market and her appraisal relies entirely on present-day comparable sales.

must_identify: the $25,000 figure was introduced first
the appraiser used independent auction databases
the appraisal did not shift toward the older insured value
the procedure was based on current comparables

title: Software license pricing
question: Was the negotiated price distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: A vendor's quote sheet lists 'Enterprise tier: $240,000/year (reference price).' The buyer's procurement team negotiates and signs at $156,000/year, calling it a 35% discount win. An industry survey shared internally shows comparable software from competitors averages $60,000 to $80,000/year for similar feature sets and seat counts.

must_identify: the $240,000 reference price came first
the final price was framed as a discount off that reference
competitor pricing was $60,000-$80,000
the final figure was pulled toward the inflated anchor

title: Two estimates compared
question: Which estimator's bid more clearly shows anchoring bias, A or B?
input: Estimator A is told the previous contractor bid $180,000 for the renovation, then submits a bid of $172,000 'just under what the last guy quoted.' Estimator B independently measures the site, prices materials and labor from current supplier catalogs, and arrives at $108,000 with no knowledge of any prior bid. Both estimators are equally experienced.

must_identify: Estimator A was given a prior reference number
A's bid was framed relative to that reference
Estimator B used independent measurement and pricing
A's bid shifted toward the anchor while B's did not

title: Doctor's smoking advice rebuttal
question: Does Marcus's reply commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Dr. Patel tells her patient Marcus that he should quit smoking because long-term studies show it dramatically increases his risk of lung cancer and heart disease. Marcus laughs and says, 'I've seen you on break behind the clinic with a cigarette in your hand. If smoking is so dangerous, you'd quit yourself. Your warning means nothing.' He then leaves without addressing the studies she cited.

must_identify: original claim concerns health risks of smoking with study evidence
reply targets the doctor's own smoking, not the evidence
inconsistency is used as grounds to dismiss the warning
the studies cited go unaddressed

title: Senator's tax reform critique
question: Does Briggs's response commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Senator Alvarez argues that the proposed tax bill will increase deficits by $400 billion over a decade, citing the Congressional Budget Office score. Senator Briggs responds: 'The CBO methodology Alvarez relies on uses static scoring that ignores growth effects. When we account for dynamic effects, the deficit impact shrinks substantially. Also, Alvarez voted for an unfunded bill in 2019.' Briggs proceeds to detail the dynamic scoring analysis.

must_identify: original claim is about deficit impact based on CBO score
Briggs substantively engages with the methodology
the hypocrisy remark is incidental, not the basis for dismissal
both elements required for tu quoque are not met

title: Parent's screen time argument
question: What rhetorical fallacy does Lin's response exhibit?
input: A mother tells her teenage daughter Lin that excessive screen time before bed disrupts sleep cycles, citing her pediatrician's recommendation and a recent sleep study. Lin replies: 'You're on your phone in bed every single night until midnight. You can't tell me to follow a rule you ignore — your argument is hypocritical and I'm not listening.' Lin doesn't engage with the pediatrician's advice or the study.

must_identify: original claim concerns sleep disruption with medical evidence
Lin attacks her mother's inconsistent behavior
hypocrisy is used as grounds to reject the advice
the underlying evidence goes unaddressed

title: Environmentalist flying critique
question: Does the blogger's reply commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Climate researcher Dr. Okafor publishes data showing that personal aviation accounts for a disproportionate share of individual carbon footprints and urges reductions in non-essential flights. A blogger replies: 'Dr. Okafor flew to three conferences last year. Until she stops flying, her call for flight reduction is meaningless and should be ignored.' The blogger does not contest the emissions data.

must_identify: original claim is empirical: aviation emissions data
reply targets Dr. Okafor's own flying behavior
inconsistency used as basis to dismiss the call
emissions data goes unrebutted

title: Chef testifying on hygiene
question: Does Hayes's challenge commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: In a health board hearing, Chef Romano testifies that he personally washes his hands between every food station, presenting it as evidence his kitchen meets sanitation standards. Inspector Hayes counters: 'Security footage from last Tuesday shows you moving from raw chicken to plated salads without washing on four separate occasions. Your testimony about your own practice is contradicted by your own conduct.' Hayes uses the footage to challenge the testimony's accuracy.

must_identify: Romano's claim is specifically about his own practice
his conduct IS the evidence in question
challenging that conduct directly engages the claim
this is a relevant character challenge, not tu quoque

title: Financial advisor savings advice
question: What fallacy does Eli commit?
input: Financial advisor Nguyen tells client Eli that contributing 15% of income to retirement accounts is mathematically necessary to retire comfortably at 65, given current return assumptions. Eli sneers: 'I happen to know you carry a $30,000 credit card balance. You can't even manage your own money. Why would I trust your math?' Eli walks out without examining the projection spreadsheet Nguyen prepared.

must_identify: original claim is a mathematical projection about savings rates
Eli attacks Nguyen's personal finances
financial inconsistency used to dismiss the calculation
the spreadsheet/math goes unexamined

title: Coach's training method dispute
question: Does Vasquez's reply commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Coach Diallo argues that his interval-training program produces better marathon times than traditional long-distance methods, citing twelve athletes' time improvements. Rival coach Vasquez replies: 'Your sample is selection-biased — you cherry-picked athletes who already showed talent for short bursts. The improvements vanish when you account for regression to the mean.' Vasquez also notes Diallo personally avoids interval workouts.

must_identify: original claim is about training program effectiveness
Vasquez engages substantively with selection bias and regression
the personal-avoidance remark is incidental
hypocrisy is not the basis for dismissal

title: Vegan ethicist's argument
question: Does the critic's response commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Philosopher Karim publishes an argument that factory-farmed meat consumption is ethically indefensible because it causes massive suffering for marginal nutritional benefit. A critic responds: 'Karim was photographed eating a cheeseburger at an airport last month. His ethical argument self-destructs — if he can't follow it, neither should anyone.' The critic offers no counterargument to the suffering-versus-benefit reasoning.

must_identify: original argument concerns ethics of factory farming
critic targets Karim's eating behavior
hypocrisy used to dismiss the ethical argument
the suffering/benefit reasoning is unaddressed

title: Two rebuttals to recycling claim
question: Which rebuttal commits the tu quoque fallacy, A or B?
input: City councilor Reyes urges expanded curbside recycling, claiming it diverts 40% of household waste from landfills based on a 2022 audit. Two responses follow. Rebuttal A: 'The audit double-counted yard waste; corrected figures show 18% diversion, not 40%.' Rebuttal B: 'Reyes throws recyclables in his regular trash — I've seen his bins. His proposal is hypocritical and shouldn't pass.' Only one is a fallacious tu quoque.

must_identify: A engages with the audit methodology directly
B targets Reyes's personal recycling behavior
B uses hypocrisy as grounds to reject the proposal
only B meets both required elements

title: Observation without dismissal
question: Does Rivka's response commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Manager Tomas tells his team that arriving on time matters because late starts cascade into missed client calls. Employee Rivka responds: 'I agree the cascade effect is real, and I'll commit to being on time. I do find it ironic, though, that you arrived at 9:20 today.' Rivka accepts the policy and the reasoning behind it; she only remarks on the irony in passing.

must_identify: Rivka accepts the substantive claim
the hypocrisy observation is not used to dismiss the claim
mere observation of inconsistency is not tu quoque
both required elements (accusation + dismissal) are absent

title: Light feathers and bright bulbs
question: Which single word is used equivocally to make the argument appear valid?
input: Consider this argument: 'Feathers are light. Anything light cannot be dark. Therefore, feathers cannot be dark.' The speaker insists the reasoning is airtight because the word 'light' appears consistently and the inference looks like a simple chain.

must_identify: the word 'light' appears in both premises
first occurrence means low in weight
second occurrence means bright or pale in color
the conclusion only follows if both senses are treated as one

title: Nothing better than eternal happiness
question: Which word shifts meaning between the two premises?
input: A philosopher argues: 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A cold sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore, a cold sandwich is better than eternal happiness.' The argument is presented as a straightforward transitive comparison, and the listener is invited to accept the conclusion on grounds of pure logic.

must_identify: 'nothing' appears in both premises
first premise uses 'nothing' as 'no thing whatsoever surpasses'
second premise uses 'nothing' as 'having no sandwich at all'
the transitive inference depends on conflating the two senses

title: Man is rational
question: Which term equivocates between the two premises?
input: An essayist writes: 'Man is the only rational animal. No woman is a man. Therefore, no woman is a rational animal.' The essayist claims the syllogism is in valid Barbara form and that rejecting the conclusion requires rejecting one of the premises outright.

must_identify: 'man' appears in both premises
first premise uses 'man' generically to mean human being
second premise uses 'man' to mean male human
the syllogism only chains if the two senses are treated identically

title: Theory in the lab
question: Which word carries two different meanings that the argument exploits?
input: A pundit claims: 'Evolution is just a theory. My coworker has a theory that the office printer is haunted. Therefore, evolution has the same epistemic status as my coworker's printer hypothesis, and neither deserves more credence than the other.' The pundit treats this as a simple application of the principle that things in the same category warrant the same treatment.

must_identify: 'theory' appears applied to evolution and to the printer
scientific 'theory' means a well-tested explanatory framework
colloquial 'theory' means a casual guess or hunch
the equivalence claim depends on collapsing both senses

title: End of life
question: Which word is used equivocally to drive the conclusion?
input: A speaker argues: 'The end of a thing is its perfection. Death is the end of life. Therefore, death is the perfection of life.' The speaker presents this as an ancient and elegant deduction, suggesting that anyone who resists the conclusion is simply uncomfortable with mortality rather than with the logic.

must_identify: 'end' appears in both premises
first 'end' means goal, purpose, or telos
second 'end' means termination or cessation
the conclusion follows only if 'end' is treated as one concept

title: Sound argument acoustics
question: Which word shifts meaning between the premises?
input: A debater says: 'Every sound argument convinces careful listeners. Whatever is sound travels through air as compression waves. Therefore, every convincing argument propagates through air as compression waves, which is why debates require good acoustics in the room.' first 'sound' means logically valid with true premises

title: Right to free speech

input: A commentator reasons: 'Whatever is right is morally good. Citizens have a right to free speech. Therefore, every exercise of free speech is morally good, and criticizing any speech act is therefore criticizing something morally good.' input: A novelist writes: 'I felt nothing when she left. Nothing is more painful than losing a loved one. Therefore, what I felt was more painful than losing a loved one, which proves I loved her deeply after all.' The novelist uses this as a paradoxical proof of hidden emotion.

must_identify: 'nothing' appears in both premises
first 'nothing' means absence of feeling
second 'nothing' means 'no thing surpasses' in a comparison
the paradoxical conclusion depends on treating the two as the same referent

title: Bank robbery loan

Therefore, my client was found near federally protected money, which justifies the heightened charges. The repeated reference to banks makes the chain self-evident.' Therefore, arsenic, hemlock, and uranium are good for you, and you should not fear them in your diet.' The blogger insists this follows from the premise that nature provides what humans need.

first 'natural' carries the loaded sense of wholesome or beneficial
second 'natural' means simply 'occurring in nature'

title: School funding speech analysis

emotional content (suffering mothers) is present
genuine evidence (audit, mortality data) directly supports effectiveness
emotion supplements rather than replaces evidence

title: Defendant's closing argument

input: Defense attorney to jury: 'My client is innocent of embezzlement. Look at him — a widower raising three small children alone, a man who served his community for twenty years, who sat in this courtroom each day with quiet dignity despite the unbearable strain on his family. Convicting him would shatter those children's lives. You cannot in good conscience send their father to prison.' support consists of sympathy for the defendant and his children
the prosecution's actual evidence is never rebutted

title: Workplace harm testimony

suffering and illness are the legitimate subject of that claim
emotional content is directly relevant evidence, not a substitute

title: Tariff policy op-ed
question: Does the op-ed commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: An op-ed argues against repealing steel tariffs: 'Picture the rust-belt towns where the mills once roared — now boarded storefronts, fathers ashamed to face their sons, churches half-empty on Sunday. Repeal would betray these proud communities who built America with their hands and sweat. Anyone who votes for repeal spits on that legacy.' title: Vaccine efficacy with anecdote

input: A pediatrician's column states: 'I still remember holding the hand of a four-year-old dying of measles complications in 1989 — a memory that haunts me. The MMR vaccine has since been studied in cohorts totaling over 1.5 million children; the Cochrane review found a 96% reduction in measles incidence among vaccinated populations and no credible association with autism across these studies. title: Zoning board appeal

title: Identify the rhetorical move

input: A lobbyist tells legislators: 'This mining regulation would close the Henderson mine. title: Two charity pitches ranked
question: Which pitch commits an appeal to emotion fallacy: A or B?
input: Pitch A: 'Donate to our literacy program. Picture a little boy who cannot read his own birthday card, his face crumpling in shame. Will you turn your back on him?' Our randomized trial across 12 schools showed participating children gained an average of 1.4 grade levels in reading within one year, compared with 0.6 in controls; one mother described her son's joy at finally reading aloud.' title: Climate policy floor speech
question: Does the senator's speech commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A senator opposing a carbon tax says: 'My colleagues parade graphs and models, but I ask you to think of Mabel, a 78-year-old widow in my district, weeping at her kitchen table over a heating bill she cannot pay. title: Mayor's curfew and crime drop
question: Does this column commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A city columnist writes: 'Mayor Hall imposed the youth curfew on June 1st. By August, juvenile arrests had fallen 22%. The curfew clearly works—before it, arrests were rising; after it, they dropped. Skeptics should look at the calendar.' The column cites no comparison cities, no enforcement data, and does not mention that schools let out for summer in early June, that a major gang leader was jailed in May, or that the police union ended a slowdown in late May.

title: Vaccine and matched controls
question: Does this brief commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: An epidemiology brief reports: 'Following the rotavirus vaccine rollout, infant hospitalizations for severe diarrhea dropped 70% in vaccinated cohorts. Researchers compared vaccinated and unvaccinated infants matched on age, region, and socioeconomic status, and biological studies show the vaccine induces neutralizing IgA antibodies in the gut. Sensitivity analyses ruled out concurrent sanitation improvements as the primary driver.' The brief explicitly attributes the decline to the vaccine.

must_identify: identifies vaccine as asserted cause and hospitalization drop as effect
notes matched comparison group is provided
notes biological mechanism (IgA antibodies) is cited
notes alternative (sanitation) was explicitly considered

title: Lucky socks and exam scores
question: Does Devon's reasoning fit the post hoc ergo propter hoc pattern? Answer yes or no.
input: Devon writes in his journal: 'I wore my green socks to the calculus midterm and got a 94. I wore them again for the chemistry final and scored a 91. The pattern is undeniable—these socks raise my test performance. From now on, every exam day means green socks.' Devon does not mention how much he studied for either exam, whether the tests were of comparable difficulty, or how he typically performs.

must_identify: identifies wearing socks as asserted cause and high scores as asserted effect

notes confounders (study time, test difficulty, baseline ability) are ignored

title: Antibiotic with mechanism cited
question: Does this note commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A clinical note reads: 'The patient's strep infection resolved within 48 hours of starting amoxicillin. Throat culture confirmed Streptococcus pyogenes, an organism whose cell wall synthesis is blocked by beta-lactam antibiotics. Repeat culture at 48 hours showed no growth. While spontaneous resolution is possible, the rapid sterilization of the culture and the matching susceptibility profile support attributing recovery to the antibiotic.'

must_identify: identifies antibiotic as asserted cause and recovery as effect
notes pharmacological mechanism (beta-lactam blocks cell wall synthesis) is cited
notes microbiological evidence (negative repeat culture) beyond mere timing
notes alternative (spontaneous resolution) is acknowledged

title: CEO hire and stock surge
question: Name the fallacy committed in one short phrase.
input: A business blog declares: 'Two weeks after Lin Patel took over as CEO, Vexor Inc.'s stock jumped 18%. Patel is clearly the catalyst the company needed. Investors should pile in—her leadership is already moving the needle.' The blog does not mention that the Federal Reserve cut rates the same week, that a competitor announced a recall the day before the surge, or that Vexor's quarterly earnings, released two weeks before Patel arrived, beat expectations.

must_identify: identifies new CEO as asserted cause, stock jump as asserted effect
notes only timing is offered as evidence
lists alternative drivers (rate cut, competitor recall, earnings beat)
names the fallacy correctly

title: Two flawed arguments compared
question: Which argument exhibits post hoc ergo propter hoc—X or Y?
input: Argument X: 'Crime and ice cream sales both peak in July across U.S. cities. Ice cream consumption fuels criminal behavior.' Argument Y: 'The town council banned plastic bags on March 1st. By June, the river cleanup volunteers reported 30% less plastic in their hauls. The ban worked.' Argument X cites no temporal precedence—just simultaneous correlation. Argument Y cites only that the ban preceded the cleanup result, with no controls or mechanism discussed.

must_identify: recognizes X is correlation without temporal-order argument (different fallacy)
recognizes Y asserts causation from temporal precedence alone
notes Y omits controls and alternative explanations
correctly selects Y

title: Comet and harvest failure
question: Does the chronicler's argument fit the post hoc ergo propter hoc pattern? Answer yes or no.
input: A medieval chronicler records: 'In the spring a great comet was seen blazing across the northern sky. That autumn the wheat harvest failed across three counties. The comet's appearance brought the famine upon us, as comets ever portend ruin.' The chronicler offers no other evidence and does not mention the unusually cold summer, the locust swarm reported in July, or the flooding of the Avon in August.

must_identify: identifies comet as asserted cause and harvest failure as effect
notes only temporal sequence is offered
lists alternative explanations (cold summer, locusts, flooding)
notes no mechanism linking comets to crops is provided

title: Diet change with controlled trial
question: Does this paper commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A nutrition paper states: 'Participants who switched to a Mediterranean diet showed a 25% reduction in cardiovascular events over five years. The randomized controlled trial assigned 7,447 participants to diet groups, controlled for age, smoking, and baseline cholesterol, and biochemical assays confirmed elevated serum omega-3 levels in the intervention arm. Investigators ruled out exercise differences via accelerometer data.' The paper attributes the reduction to dietary change.

must_identify: identifies diet as asserted cause and cardiovascular reduction as effect
notes randomization and controls
notes biochemical mechanism evidence (omega-3 levels)
notes alternative (exercise) explicitly ruled out

title: Software update and crashes
question: Does the manager's reasoning commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: An IT manager emails the team: 'We pushed update 4.2 on Tuesday morning. By Thursday, helpdesk tickets for application crashes had tripled. The update is the culprit—roll it back immediately.' The email does not mention that a Windows security patch deployed Wednesday night, that a major customer onboarded 400 new users Thursday, or that the load balancer was reconfigured Tuesday afternoon by the network team.

must_identify: identifies update 4.2 as asserted cause and crash spike as effect
notes the link is purely sequential
lists confounders (Windows patch, user onboarding, load balancer change)
notes no log analysis or mechanism cited

title: Rooster and the sunrise
question: Name the specific fallacy in this argument.
input: A child argues: 'Every morning the rooster crows, and then the sun rises. I have watched this for a whole month—first the rooster, then the sun. Therefore the rooster's crowing causes the sunrise.' The child offers no other evidence and considers no alternative explanation for why the sun rises.

must_identify: identifies crowing as asserted cause and sunrise as asserted effect
notes only temporal precedence is cited
notes no mechanism is offered
names the fallacy

title: Museum trustee's authority claim
question: Is the trustee's argument for her authority circular? Answer yes or no.
input: The museum's chief trustee defended her sole authority to deaccession artifacts: 'My decisions about deaccessioning cannot be overruled because I hold final authority over collection matters. And we know I hold final authority over collection matters precisely because no one has the standing to overrule my deaccessioning decisions.' She added that the museum was founded in 1887 and currently houses 12,000 objects, statistics frequently cited in annual reports.

must_identify: conclusion: trustee has unoverrulable authority over deaccessioning
premise that authority exists is supported by the inability to overrule
inability to overrule is supported by her authority
founding date and object count are distractors, not grounds
the loop closes within the quoted passage

title: Reliable witness testimony loop
question: What flaw best describes counsel's reasoning about Polson's reliability?
input: Defense counsel argued: 'Witness Polson should be believed because he is reliable. We know he is reliable because his testimony in this case matches what actually happened, and we know his testimony matches what happened because Polson, a reliable witness, said so.' The court also heard that Polson has lived in the district for 22 years and volunteers at a local shelter on weekends.

must_identify: conclusion: Polson is reliable / should be believed
premise: his testimony matches reality
that premise is supported only by his own reliable say-so
residency and volunteering are biographical distractors
no independent corroboration is offered

title: Sacred text self-authentication
question: Does the pamphlet commit circular reasoning?
input: A pamphlet argues: 'The Codex of Liriel is divinely inspired because it states on its first page that it is the word of the goddess. We can trust that statement because anything written in a divinely inspired text must be true.' The pamphlet also notes the Codex contains 4,000 verses, has been translated into nine languages, and is read aloud at every harvest festival in the region.

must_identify: conclusion: the Codex is divinely inspired
premise: the Codex says it is divinely inspired
trust in the statement requires already accepting divine inspiration
verse count, translations, and festival use are distractors
the justification loop is fully contained in the argument

title: Drug efficacy from independent trial
question: Does the reviewer's argument for XR-7's efficacy commit circular reasoning?
input: A reviewer wrote: 'Compound XR-7 lowers blood pressure effectively. In a randomized double-blind trial of 1,200 patients conducted by an independent lab, systolic pressure dropped an average of 14 mmHg in the treatment group versus 2 mmHg in the placebo group over twelve weeks. The manufacturer also strongly endorses the compound and has marketed it aggressively since 2019.'

must_identify: conclusion: XR-7 effectively lowers blood pressure
premise: independent randomized trial showing measured drop
trial evidence is external to the conclusion
manufacturer endorsement is a separate weak appeal, not circularity
no premise presupposes the conclusion

title: Best chef in town
question: Identify the reasoning flaw in the blogger's main argument.
input: A food blogger insists: 'Chef Aren is the best chef in Brindle. The proof is that he runs the town's finest restaurant. How do we know it's the finest? Because no other restaurant in Brindle is run by a chef as skilled as Aren.' The blogger adds that Aren trained in Lyon for three years and won a regional competition in 2018, facts mentioned only briefly at the end.

must_identify: conclusion: Aren is the best chef
premise: he runs the finest restaurant
finest restaurant claim relies on Aren being most skilled
Lyon training and competition are independent but not used as the main support
the main argument loops without using the external credentials

title: Free market efficiency claim
question: Is the op-ed's central argument for free-market efficiency circular?
input: An op-ed states: 'Free markets allocate resources efficiently. We see this because in a free market, prices reflect true value, and prices reflect true value precisely because efficient allocation is what free markets achieve.' The author also references a 2003 study by Hartwell on agricultural subsidies, though the study is mentioned only to introduce the topic and is not used to support the efficiency claim.

must_identify: conclusion: free markets allocate efficiently
premise: prices reflect true value
that premise is justified by efficient allocation itself
the Hartwell study is not used as supporting evidence here
no external grounding breaks the loop

title: Bridge safety inspection report
question: Does the memo's argument for the bridge's safety commit circular reasoning?
input: An engineer's memo concludes: 'The Halberd Street bridge is safe for vehicles up to 30 tons. Strain gauges installed last month recorded peak loads of 28 tons during rush hour with deflection of 3mm, well within the 12mm tolerance specified by the original 1974 design code. The mayor, who frequently crosses the bridge, has publicly praised the engineering team for their thoroughness.'

must_identify: conclusion: the bridge is safe for 30-ton loads
premise: measured strain data within design tolerance
design code provides independent external standard
mayor's praise is irrelevant flattery, not circular support
no premise presupposes the safety conclusion

title: Gifted student selection committee
question: What is the reasoning flaw in the memo's defense of the program?
input: A school memo defends its gifted program: 'Students in our gifted program are exceptionally talented. We know this because they were selected by our rigorous committee, and the committee is rigorous because it consistently identifies exceptionally talented students.' The memo also notes that 62% of program graduates attend four-year colleges and that the program has operated since 1991, statistics offered as background context.

must_identify: conclusion: gifted students are exceptionally talented
premise: committee selected them
committee's rigor justified by selecting talented students
college statistics are background, not used to support rigor
the loop closes between talent and committee judgment

title: Heirloom tomato superiority debate
question: Does the farmer's argument commit circular reasoning?
input: A farmer claims: 'Heirloom tomatoes taste better than hybrids. In a blind taste test conducted by the county fair last August, 73 of 100 randomly selected attendees preferred heirloom samples, and trained sommeliers rated their flavor complexity 4.2 versus 3.1 on a standardized scale. Many heirloom enthusiasts also feel passionately that their preferred varieties are simply the best.'

must_identify: conclusion: heirlooms taste better than hybrids
premise: blind taste test results and sommelier ratings
evidence is external to the conclusion
enthusiast passion is mentioned but not used as proof
no premise presupposes the taste conclusion

title: Captain's leadership justification
question: Is the officer's main argument circular?
input: A naval officer argues: 'Captain Vellis deserves command of the flagship because she possesses superior leadership. Her superior leadership is evident from her holding the flagship command, since only superior leaders are entrusted with that vessel.' The officer mentions that Vellis served twelve years at sea and graduated second in her academy class, but presents these as biographical asides rather than reasons for the command decision.

must_identify: conclusion: Vellis deserves flagship command
premise: she has superior leadership
leadership claim grounded in already holding command
service record and academy ranking presented as asides, not main support
the principal justification loops

title: Tourist judges city drivers
question: Does Marcus's reasoning commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: Marcus visited Rome for a four-day vacation last summer. During his stay, he was nearly hit by a scooter in the historic center, watched two cars run a red light near the Colosseum, and saw a taxi cut off a pedestrian outside his hotel. Back home, he tells his friends with full confidence: 'Italians are reckless drivers. All of them. I saw it firsthand.' He adds that anyone planning to drive in Italy should expect chaos from every motorist on the road.

must_identify: claim covers all Italian drivers
evidence is a handful of incidents in one tourist district
four days in one city is unrepresentative of a national population
selection bias: tourist centers attract aggressive driving

title: Surveyed pharmacists nationwide
question: Does the lead author's conclusion commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: A public health team randomly surveyed 8,200 licensed pharmacists across all 50 states over six months, weighting responses by region and practice setting. Based on the results, the lead author writes: 'Most American pharmacists report feeling burned out by current staffing levels.' A blog summarizing the study warns readers that the profession is in crisis and that staffing reform is urgent. The blog's author has never worked in a pharmacy and relies entirely on the survey data for the claim.

must_identify: sample size is large (8,200)
sampling was random and weighted across states
scope of claim ('most American pharmacists') matches sample scope
author's lack of experience is a distractor, not a sampling flaw

title: Hedged opinion on novels
question: Does Priya commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: After finishing three contemporary literary novels recommended by a friend, Priya posts a short review: 'In my experience, these three books all leaned heavily on unreliable narrators. I'm starting to suspect this is a trend in current literary fiction, but I've only read a small slice and could easily be wrong. I'd be curious whether wider readers have noticed the same pattern.' She invites comments and links to the three titles she read.

must_identify: Priya hedges with 'in my experience' and 'small slice'
she explicitly acknowledges she could be wrong
no universal or population-level claim is asserted
hedged generalizations are excluded by the skill's constraints

title: Two coworkers and remote work
question: What specific reasoning flaw does Devon's memo exhibit?
input: Devon manages a team of forty. Two of his direct reports, Alia and Brent, missed deadlines after switching to remote work last quarter. In a memo to the executive board, Devon writes: 'Remote workers cannot be trusted to meet deadlines. Productivity collapses without office oversight, and our company should immediately end all work-from-home arrangements across every department.' He cites Alia and Brent as the basis for his recommendation and does not reference any other data, internal or external.

must_identify: claim covers all remote workers across every department
evidence is only two employees
sample size is far too small for the company-wide conclusion
no controls for other causes of missed deadlines

title: Dog breed temperament claim
question: Does Helena's conclusion commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: Helena's neighbor owns a border collie that nipped her son during a backyard visit last weekend. The next day, a second border collie at the dog park barked aggressively at her stroller. Helena tells the parenting forum: 'Border collies are dangerous around children. Every parent should avoid the breed entirely. I've now seen what they're really like.' Several commenters ask whether she has interacted with other border collies; she replies that these two encounters were enough to convince her.

must_identify: claim covers the entire breed
evidence is two individual dogs
sample is far too small for breed-wide conclusion
context (one neighborhood, two days) is narrow

title: Celebrity endorses supplement
question: Is the ad's primary reasoning flaw hasty generalization, or a different fallacy?
input: An Olympic swimmer appears in an advertisement holding a bottle of magnesium supplements. 'I take these every morning, and so should you,' she says. 'Trust me — I'm a world-class athlete and I know what works for the human body.' The ad runs during prime time and the brand reports a sales spike. A consumer advocate writes a column criticizing the ad's reasoning, arguing that the swimmer's endorsement does not establish that the supplements are effective for the general public.

must_identify: the ad relies on the swimmer's authority/celebrity status
this is an appeal to authority, not a generalization from a sample
skill constraints exclude conflating with appeals to authority
no explicit small-sample-to-population leap is being made

title: Three students and the textbook
question: What is the specific gap that makes Han's leap unjustified — sample size, selection bias, or context?
input: Professor Han asked three students after class what they thought of the new statistics textbook. All three said the chapters were confusing. At the next faculty meeting, Han recommends pulling the book from the curriculum, telling colleagues: 'Students universally find this text unreadable. The whole cohort is struggling and we owe them a replacement immediately.' The class enrolls 240 students. Han did not survey the others or review exam performance before making his recommendation.

must_identify: claim is about the entire 240-student cohort
evidence is only three students
primary gap is the tiny sample relative to population
the three may also be self-selected, but size is the central deficit

title: Online forum members on parenting
question: What specific gap makes the journalist's leap unjustified — sample size, selection bias, or context?
input: A journalist spends a month reading posts on a single online forum dedicated to parents who chose not to vaccinate their children. She notes that the overwhelming majority of posters express deep distrust of pediatricians. She publishes a feature claiming: 'American parents have lost faith in pediatric medicine. Trust in doctors has collapsed nationwide.' The forum has roughly 12,000 active members. The article does not mention any broader survey or comparison group, and the forum's membership criteria are stated openly on its homepage.

must_identify: claim is about American parents generally
sample is drawn entirely from an anti-vaccination forum
forum members are self-selected and unrepresentative
size (12,000) is not the issue; the bias in who was sampled is

title: Single bad meal one location
question: Does Tomas's review commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: Tomas ordered delivery from the downtown branch of a regional burger chain on a rainy Tuesday night. The fries arrived soggy and the burger was lukewarm. He posts a one-star review on a national review site with the headline: 'This entire chain serves garbage food. Avoid every location in the country.' The chain operates 78 restaurants across four states. Tomas has never visited any other location and ordered only once from the downtown branch.

must_identify: claim covers all 78 locations chain-wide
evidence is a single delivery order from one branch
one meal cannot represent an entire chain
context (rainy night, delivery) could explain the food quality

title: Census of village wells
question: Does the engineer's reported conclusion commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: A water-quality engineer tested every one of the 47 wells in a small mountain village over two weeks, following a protocol audited by the regional health authority. Twenty-nine wells exceeded the safe limit for arsenic. She reports to the village council: 'A majority of wells in this village are contaminated above the safe threshold.' A council member objects that she only sampled wells in this village and shouldn't make sweeping claims, urging her to retract the report before it alarms residents.

must_identify: claim is restricted to wells in this village
she sampled every well (a full census)
scope of claim matches scope of evidence exactly
council member's objection misreads the claim's scope

title: Rare disease screening conclusion
question: Does Dr. Pell's reasoning commit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A new blood test for Welton's syndrome is 99% accurate: it correctly flags 99% of people with the disease and gives a positive result in only 1% of healthy people. Welton's syndrome occurs in roughly 1 in 10,000 adults. Dr. Pell tells her patient Marco, who has no symptoms but tested positive in a routine workplace screening, that he almost certainly has Welton's syndrome because the test is so accurate.

must_identify: the test accuracy (99%) is the case-specific evidence
the prior prevalence (1 in 10,000) is stated and very low
with such a low prior, false positives vastly outnumber true positives
the conclusion relies only on accuracy and ignores the prior

title: Terrorist facial recognition camera
question: Does the security chief's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: An airport facial-recognition system identifies known terrorists with 99.5% sensitivity and a 0.5% false-positive rate. Intelligence estimates that about 1 in 1,000,000 travelers passing through is on the watchlist. After the system flags traveler Anya, the security chief announces, 'Given the system's 99.5% accuracy, we are virtually certain Anya is a watchlisted terrorist and will detain her accordingly.'

must_identify: the case-specific evidence is the system flagging Anya
the prior probability (1 in 1,000,000) is extremely low
a 0.5% false-positive rate produces ~5,000 false flags per million
true positives are dwarfed by false positives, contradicting the chief's certainty

title: Drunk driver breath test
question: Does Officer Reyes's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: On a Saturday night near a sports stadium, police data show that roughly 1 in 4 drivers leaving the area are over the legal alcohol limit. A breathalyzer used at the checkpoint is 90% accurate in both directions. Officer Reyes stops driver Kim, who blows positive. Reyes notes: 'Given that one in four drivers here is drunk and the test is 90% accurate, the positive result strongly suggests Kim is over the limit, though we'll confirm with a blood test.'

must_identify: the case-specific evidence is Kim's positive breath test
the prior (1 in 4) is explicitly mentioned and is not low
Reyes acknowledges both the prior and the test accuracy
the conclusion is appropriately hedged and uses both pieces of information

title: Spam filter flag certainty
question: Does the IT lead's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: An enterprise spam filter correctly classifies 98% of spam as spam and only 2% of legitimate mail as spam. In this firm's mail stream, about 70% of incoming messages are spam. The IT lead writes in a memo: 'Whenever the filter marks a message as spam, the 98% accuracy rate means we should be very confident the message is indeed spam before deletion, but legitimate mail is common enough that we still review the quarantine.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence is the filter flag
the prior (70% spam) is explicitly considered
the reasoning acknowledges both rates
because the prior is high, confidence in a flag is reasonable; no neglect

title: Steroid test for Olympians
question: Does the federation's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A doping panel uses a urine assay that correctly identifies steroid users 95% of the time and yields a false positive in 3% of clean athletes. Audit data from past Games estimate that about 2% of competing athletes actually used banned steroids. Sprinter Lopez tests positive. The federation's press release states: 'Because the test is 95% accurate, we have overwhelming evidence Lopez was doping, and a lifetime ban is appropriate.'

must_identify: the case-specific evidence is Lopez's positive test
the prior (2% steroid use) is stated and low
a 3% false-positive rate on 98% clean athletes outweighs true positives from 2% users
the press release ignores the prior and concludes from accuracy alone

title: Mammogram screening claim
question: Does the radiologist's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A radiologist explains to a 40-year-old patient: 'Mammograms detect about 80% of existing breast cancers and produce false positives in roughly 10% of women without cancer. At your age, the chance of having breast cancer in any given year is about 0.4%. Your screening came back positive, so although that is concerning, the actual probability you have cancer given this result is still under 5%, and we'll need a follow-up biopsy.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence is the positive mammogram
the prior (0.4%) is explicitly stated and used
the radiologist computes a posterior that incorporates both

title: Geological mineral indicator
question: Which reasoning flaw, if any, does the CEO commit?
input: A geophysical survey instrument detects buried lithium deposits with 92% sensitivity and a 4% false alarm rate. Across the surveyed region, prior drilling suggests roughly 1 plot in 500 actually contains commercially viable lithium. After the instrument signals plot 47-B, the prospecting firm's CEO declares: 'The instrument is 92% accurate, so we are confident plot 47-B contains lithium and we will commit drilling capital this quarter.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence: the instrument signal at 47-B
prior of 1 in 500 is stated and low
4% false-alarm rate on 499 empty plots produces many false signals per true
the CEO uses only sensitivity and ignores the prior

title: Lie detector courtroom argument
question: Does the prosecutor's argument exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A prosecutor argues: 'The polygraph correctly identifies liars 88% of the time and falsely accuses truth-tellers 12% of the time. The defendant failed the polygraph when asked whether he was at the warehouse. Given the test's 88% accuracy, the jury should conclude the defendant was lying.' The prosecutor offers no information about how often defendants in similar cases actually lie about such matters.

must_identify: case-specific evidence is the failed polygraph
no prior frequency is provided in the passage
the skill requires a stated or strongly implied prior to flag neglect
argument may be weak for other reasons but does not meet the criteria for base-rate neglect as defined

title: Genetic ancestry match
question: Does the lab's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A genealogy lab markets a marker that appears in 99% of people with Viking ancestry and only 2% of people without. In the Scottish town being tested, historical records suggest about 0.5% of residents have any Viking ancestry. Customer Hamish carries the marker; the lab's report tells him: 'Because our marker test is 99% accurate, you almost certainly descend from Vikings.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence is Hamish's marker
the prior (0.5% Viking ancestry locally) is stated and low
2% false-positive rate among the 99.5% non-Viking majority swamps true positives
the conclusion uses only the accuracy figure

title: Predictive maintenance sensor
question: Does Ortiz's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A factory's vibration sensor flags imminent bearing failures with 96% sensitivity and a 5% false-alarm rate. Maintenance records show that on any given day, only about 1 in 2,000 bearings is actually about to fail. When sensor 12 flags bearing #44, plant manager Ortiz writes in her log: 'Even though the sensor is 96% accurate, bearing failures are rare enough that most flags turn out to be false alarms — I'll inspect, but I'm not shutting down the line yet.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence is sensor 12's flag
the prior (1 in 2,000) is explicitly stated
Ortiz integrates both rates in her judgment
appropriate caution reflects use, not neglect, of the prior

title: Shark attack vacation fear
question: Does Marcus's risk estimate exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: After watching a week-long cable news series featuring three vivid shark attack reconstructions, Marcus cancels his beach vacation. He tells his sister, 'Shark attacks must be happening constantly now—I can picture exactly how they unfold.' His sister shows him an International Shark File report indicating annual unprovoked attacks worldwide have remained between 60 and 80 for the past decade, with no spike this year. Marcus insists the risk has clearly risen and books a mountain cabin instead. He notes the news producer interviewed survivors with graphic detail.

must_identify: Marcus estimates shark attack frequency based on vivid recalled news segments
the Shark File statistics show stable base rates contradicting his estimate
ease of recall (graphic survivor interviews) drives the judgment
mismatch between recall-based estimate and cited base rate

title: Epidemiologist registry argument
question: Does Dr. Patel's frequency claim exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: Dr. Patel reviews her clinic's diagnostic patterns and concludes that Lyme disease is being overdiagnosed locally. She cites the state health department registry showing an incidence of 4.2 cases per 100,000 in her county, while her clinic alone reports a rate equivalent to 31 per 100,000 among its patient population. She acknowledges that several recent memorable cases—including a colleague's child—came to mind while preparing the analysis, but bases her conclusion on the registry comparison and patient demographic adjustments.

must_identify: Patel's claim is grounded in registry incidence statistics
vivid recalled cases are mentioned but not the basis of the estimate
no mismatch between her conclusion and the cited base rate
skill rule: don't flag estimates correctly grounded in statistics

title: Lottery winner neighbor
question: Does Elena's probability judgment exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: Elena's neighbor won a $40,000 scratch-off prize last month, and her cousin won $200 on a different ticket two weeks later. Elena now buys ten tickets a week, telling her husband, 'People around here win all the time—it's clearly more likely than people think.' Her husband points to the state lottery's published odds: 1 in 3.2 million for the top prize, 1 in 4 for any prize over $1. Elena waves this off, citing the two recent wins she personally witnessed as proof the odds 'feel different in practice.'

must_identify: Elena estimates winning likelihood from two personally witnessed instances

title: Actuary mortality table review
question: Does Hannah's revised estimate exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: Senior actuary Hannah revises upward her firm's mortality estimate for motorcyclists aged 18-25 after a quarterly review. She recalls two high-profile fatal crashes from the previous month that she read about in trade publications. However, her revision is based on the latest NHTSA fatality-per-mile data showing a 12% increase in the cohort, cross-referenced with three insurance industry actuarial tables that confirm the trend. She documents that the recalled crashes prompted the review but did not determine the magnitude of the revision.

must_identify: Hannah's revision magnitude is grounded in NHTSA and actuarial data
recalled crashes triggered review but didn't determine the estimate
no mismatch between conclusion and statistical evidence
vivid recall alone doesn't constitute availability bias when data drives the number

title: Kidnapping news cycle parent
question: Does Raj's frequency estimate exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: After three nationally televised child abduction cases dominate headlines for two weeks, Raj forbids his ten-year-old from walking to school. He tells the PTA, 'Stranger kidnappings are clearly an epidemic—I can name three off the top of my head.' A school counselor presents FBI NCIC data showing stereotypical stranger abductions number around 100 per year nationally among 74 million children, a rate stable for fifteen years. Raj responds that statistics don't capture what's really happening and points again to the recent cases.

must_identify: Raj estimates abduction frequency from recalled news cases
FBI NCIC base rate contradicts the 'epidemic' claim
media salience drives ease of recall and the estimate
Raj explicitly rejects statistics in favor of memorable instances

title: Startled hiker bear encounter
question: Does Tomas's reaction exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: While hiking, Tomas hears a branch snap and freezes, his heart pounding. He thinks, 'That could be a bear.' He does not estimate how often bears appear on this trail or whether bear encounters are common in the region. After a moment he sees a deer, exhales, and continues walking. Later at the lodge he tells friends he was scared but doesn't claim bears are unusually frequent or rare; he simply describes the startle.

must_identify: Tomas has an emotional fear response, not a frequency claim
no probability or likelihood estimate is asserted
skill rule: don't flag mere fear responses without frequency claims

title: Plane crash news commuter
question: What cognitive bias does Brenda's reasoning illustrate?
input: Following extensive coverage of two commercial aviation incidents, Brenda cancels her flight from Chicago to Denver and rents a car for the 1,000-mile drive. She tells her coworker, 'Flying is just too risky right now—I keep seeing these crashes everywhere.' Her coworker references NTSB data: commercial aviation fatalities per passenger-mile remain roughly 1/100th those of automobile travel, and the cited incidents did not change the trend. Brenda replies that she cannot get the images out of her head and feels safer behind the wheel.

must_identify: Brenda judges flying risk by ease of recalling vivid news images
NTSB statistics show driving is far more dangerous per mile
mismatch between recall-based judgment and statistical base rate
media-driven salience as the source of the recall

title: Quality engineer defect rate
question: Does Soo-jin's frequency claim exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: Quality engineer Soo-jin reports that defect rates on Line 3 have risen this quarter. Her finding draws on the SPC control chart logs showing defects per thousand units climbing from 2.1 to 3.8, a deviation flagged by automatic statistical alarms. She mentions that one particularly memorable defective batch—where a customer complained loudly—made her start looking, but the increase she reports is the chart's measured value, independently verified by a second engineer using a different sampling protocol.

must_identify: Soo-jin's rate is grounded in SPC chart measurements
memorable batch triggered investigation but didn't set the rate

title: Shooting coverage urban danger
question: Does Greta's frequency claim exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: After local news runs a four-night series on three downtown shootings, Greta tells her book club that violent crime in their city has 'exploded' and avoids going downtown. She cites the three cases by name and a fourth she heard about from a friend. The city's annual Uniform Crime Report, released the same week, shows violent crime rates have declined 8% year-over-year and are at a 20-year low. Greta says the report 'must be cooking the numbers' because she knows what she's seen on TV.

must_identify: Greta judges crime frequency by recalled news cases
UCR data contradicts the 'exploded' claim, showing decline
media salience drives ease of recall
Greta dismisses the statistical evidence in favor of vivid memories

title: Doctor antibiotic resistance estimate
question: Does Dr. Yusuf's frequency claim exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: Dr. Yusuf tells a resident that MRSA infections in their hospital have become 'the dominant staph variant we're seeing.' Pressed for evidence, he names four memorable patients from the last month and a journal article he skimmed about rising resistance nationally. The hospital's microbiology surveillance dashboard, which he has not consulted in three months, actually shows MRSA accounts for 18% of staph isolates locally—down from 24% a year prior. The resident pulls up the dashboard and shows him the figures.

must_identify: Yusuf estimates MRSA dominance from four recalled patients
surveillance dashboard shows 18% (a minority), contradicting 'dominant'
ease of recall of memorable cases drives the estimate
mismatch in direction between recall-based claim and base-rate data

title: Failed pharma trial continuation
question: Does the CFO's reasoning exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Helix Pharma's Phase II trial of drug HX-7 missed both primary endpoints, and the independent monitoring board projects under 8% chance of Phase III success. The CFO argues at the board meeting: 'We've poured $340 million and four years into HX-7. Pulling the plug now would waste all of that. We have to push into Phase III.' The board has a viable alternative: terminate HX-7 and redirect funds to a promising oncology candidate. The CFO's recommendation prevails.

must_identify: forward-looking evidence is negative (8% success, missed endpoints)
justification cites $340M and four years already spent
viable alternative (oncology candidate) exists
prior spend is treated as a reason to continue rather than unrecoverable

title: Restaurant remodel with strong forecasts
question: Does Priya's decision exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Owner Priya has spent $180,000 and eight months remodeling her bistro. New foot-traffic studies and pre-bookings indicate the remodeled space will gross 40% more annually than the old layout, with payback inside two years. Priya tells her partner, 'Yes, we've sunk a lot in already, but more importantly the projections show this will earn out quickly. Let's finish it.' She approves the final $25,000 of work.

must_identify: forward-looking evidence is positive (40% gross increase, fast payback)
prior spend is mentioned but not the primary justification
continuation is supported by future expected value
the pattern requires non-positive forward outlook, which is absent

title: Concert ticket in blizzard
question: Does Marcus's reasoning exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Marcus paid $220 for a non-refundable concert ticket three weeks ago. On the night of the show, a blizzard warning is issued; police advise no non-essential travel, the venue says doors will still open, and Marcus has a bad cold. He tells his roommate, 'I don't really feel up to it and the drive looks dangerous, but $220 is $220 — I'm going.' He could stay home at no additional cost.

must_identify: forward outlook is negative (illness, dangerous travel)
justification rests on the $220 already spent
staying home is a viable alternative
the $220 is unrecoverable regardless of attendance

title: Forced bond completion
question: Does the CEO's reasoning exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Acme Construction is 60% through a municipal bridge contract. New cost overruns mean Acme will lose $4M completing the work. The contract's performance bond legally compels completion; walking away triggers $12M in penalties and bars Acme from future state bids. The CEO says, 'We'll lose money finishing, but the bond and disqualification make stopping far worse. We complete the bridge.'

must_identify: the actor is contractually compelled to continue
abandonment is not a viable alternative due to bond and disqualification
justification is forward-looking comparison of penalties
prior spend is not the basis of the decision

title: PhD student switching fields
question: Does Lena's reasoning exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Lena is in year five of a PhD on a topic her advisor now agrees is a dead end; recent papers have scooped her core contribution and her committee estimates under 15% chance of a defensible thesis on the current path. Her department offers her a switch to a related project with strong prospects. Lena says, 'I've put five years into this. I can't throw that away. I'm sticking with the original topic,' and declines the switch.

must_identify: forward outlook is poor (scooped, <15% defensible)
justification cites five years already invested
viable alternative project is offered and declined
the five years is sunk regardless of choice

title: Two reasons for continuing mine
question: Does the board's decision exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A copper mine has consumed $90M over a decade. Recent assays revealed an unexpectedly rich vein; engineers project the mine will yield $300M in profit over its remaining life. The board votes to continue operations. The chair states: 'We've invested too much to walk away now, and frankly the new assay numbers make this the most profitable site in our portfolio.'

although prior spend is mentioned, independent positive future value justifies continuation
the skill requires non-positive forward expected value

title: Failing startup pivot refusal

input: Founder Theo's social-app startup has burned $6M with declining users for nine consecutive months; market analysts estimate runway-to-profitability probability at near zero on the current product. justification cites $6M already spent
viable pivot alternative with funding is offered
sunk $6M does not change with continuation

title: All-you-can-eat overeating

input: Diego paid $35 for an all-you-can-eat buffet. After three plates he is uncomfortably full and feels slightly ill. He surveys the dessert table and thinks, 'I paid $35, so I need to keep eating to get my money's worth,' and serves himself a fourth plate despite no longer enjoying the food.

justification cites the $35 already paid
stopping is a viable alternative

title: Acknowledged unrecoverable training cost
question: Does Hannah's reasoning exhibit the sunk-cost fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Coach Hannah spent two seasons developing quarterback Reese, who has shown no improvement and whose metrics rank lowest in the league. A trade window opens. decision is based on forward-looking comparison

title: Two manager memos compared

input: Memo A (VP Singh): 'We've poured 14 months and $2M into Project Atlas. Even though the latest user tests show customers won't pay for it, we cannot waste that investment. Continue funding.'
